commits.message:
test(docs): gate the two lies a machine can catch, and name the one it cannot (rich-docs-site-13t.6) (#86)

* test(docs): gate the two lies a machine can catch, and name the one it cannot

Adds the last child of the docs-site epic: a check that every symbol the
documentation names exists, and every page the site ships is reachable.

REACHABILITY is a set equality with no exclusions. `docs/strip.md` was
unreachable for four commits because the sidebar was a hand-copied list and
nobody could see the drift by reading either file. The page-backed regions move
to `docs/.vitepress/sidebar.ts` so the test can import the site's own list
rather than a copy of it — `config.ts` reads the gitignored `demos.json` at
module load, so importing that file from the unit suite would throw on a fresh
clone. The Demos region stays behind: its links are dynamic routes, not
`docs/*.md`, and comparing them against pages on disk would need an exclusion
predicate nobody rechecks.

SYMBOL EXISTENCE is checked two ways — a name imported from an entry point, and
a member called on a class the page itself constructed. The second is what
catches the transliteration defects, since six of this epic's confirmed ghosts
were methods rather than imports. Both derive from `package.json#exports`
through the coverage gate's own `deriveEntryModules`, now returning specifier →
source rather than discarding the specifier, so "exists" means the same thing in
both directions.

WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT DO. It does not compile the blocks. That was
measured, not assumed: extracting all 211 and type-checking them one file apiece
yields 145 failures, and reading the first failure on each of the 25 pages shows
the overwhelming majority are genre artifacts — a page is a running document
(`markup.md` calls `console.print` five sections before constructing its
`Console`) and a page elides (`doStep`, `riskyOperation`, `items`). Going green
on those would tax every future page for its elisions.

The blocks are parsed, never pattern-matched. The regex version reported four
defects that were not defects — `docs/tree.md` builds a file tree containing the
string "console.test.ts", `docs/console.md` opens with `// shared/console.ts` —
and a check that invents findings is worse than no check.

THE GATE FOUND 13 REAL GHOSTS ON THREE PAGES NOBODY HAD AUDITED, all verified
against source and by execution before being touched:

- progress.md: `run()` documented as the primary lifecycle idiom (does not
  exist; `start`/`stop` do), `update` (it is `updateTask`), `open`/`wrapFile`
  (an entire file-reading section for an absent capability), five of eleven
  listed columns, and `getRenderable`.
- live.md: `run()`, `screen: true` (the option is `altScreen`), and
  `new Table("Job", "Status")` (the constructor takes an options object).
- layout.md: `tree`, plus `new Layout("name")` — which sets the pane's CONTENT,
  not its name — and `layout["name"]`, which no index signature supports.

Every replacement was run before it was written down. `Table.addColumn` takes
its header positionally, not as an options object; I assumed otherwise and the
runtime said no, which is the whole argument for executing rather than reading.

Closes rich-docs-site-dl4, whose three named live.md defects are these.
Filed rich-docs-site-9dz (layout.md's fabricated output blocks and its false
empty-layout premise) and rich-table-5m9 (`addRow` does not parse markup, while
`addColumn` does).

THE CEILING IS NAMED IN THE TEST'S OWN HEADER, because a green bar here will be
read as "these pages are true" otherwise. Symbol existence is the weakest of the
three ways a page lies. On console.md it would have caught six ghosts; on
strip.md it would have caught nothing, and all six defects there were real —
provenance decides which, since a page transliterated from Python inherits
Python's API surface while a page written alongside its subsystem lies about
behavior instead. Classes 2 (the symbol exists and does something else) and 3
(a true claim about one path, generalized over the surface) stay a reviewer's job.

Every failure arm is verified by injection, not by assertion: fictional import,
ghost member, unlinked page, dangling link, duplicate link.

* test(docs): resolve the receiver instead of recognizing one shape of it

Addresses 5 of 10 review findings on PR #86. The one that mattered: extractMemberUses recorded a use only when the receiver was a bare identifier, so layout.getByName(name)! was dropped entirely — a blind spot I introduced in this same PR by rewriting docs/layout.md to that pattern. The receiver now travels as data (root class + method path) and the test layer resolves each hop through the method's declared return type; a ghost on the chained form now fails and names Layout. Also: position-aware binding (strip.md redeclares strip as Strip then FlexStrip; nearest-preceding, else nearest-following, which keeps markup.md's forward reference working), resolveAlias reused from coverage/extract.ts instead of a one-hop copy, ambiguous class names reported rather than silently overwritten, unclosed fences throw, and one ts.createProgram instead of two.

Still open, planned on their threads: CLAUDE.md points at config.ts for guideSidebar; progress.md's updateTask({total}), {speed} field, and TextColumn format string; layout.md's placeholder premise and fabricated output blocks.

* docs: three pages that described a library this port does not have

Addresses the last 4 of 10 review findings on PR #86, all of them the same
defect in different places: prose asserting a capability the source does not
implement.

CLAUDE.md sent contributors to `docs/.vitepress/config.ts` for `guideSidebar`,
which this PR moved to `sidebar.ts`. That instruction is exactly how the second,
competing definition gets written — the failure the paragraph itself is about.
It now names the right file, says why the split exists (config.ts reads the
gitignored demos.json at module load, so the unit suite cannot import it), and
points at the check that fails on drift.

progress.md documented three things that do not exist. `updateTask(task, {total})`
and `updateTask(task, {speed})` are both excess-property errors — TaskUpdateOptions
is completed/advance/description/visible/refresh, and no `fields` map or index
signature stores custom data. The format-string example reached further than the
finding said: TextColumn.render does one `.replace(/\{task\.description\}/g, …)`,
so the documented "{task.description} [{task.completed}/{task.total}]
{task.fields[speed]}" renders three of its four placeholders as literal braces.
The whole "Indeterminate progress" section was fabricated — `total: null` does not
type-check against `total?: number`, and a task with no total renders a bar stuck
at 0%, verified by running it, not a pulse. Per the epic's direction the page
yields to the code, so the section is replaced by the real adjacent capability it
was half-using: `start: false` plus `startTask()`, deferring the clock rather than
the total.

layout.md claimed an empty layout renders a placeholder box with its name and
dimensions, and drew two output blocks showing them. `render()` yields only
`if (this._renderable)`, so a content-less leaf emits zero bytes; both pictures
were Python Rich's placeholder rendering, which this port does not implement.
Both examples now assign content, and both output blocks are bytes captured from
a run rather than redrawn. `console.print(root, { height: 6 })` nearly went in
with them — it ran and produced the right output, and PrintOptions has no
`height`. Executing an example proves the output; only the type proves the call.

Closes rich-docs-site-9dz, which was filed for layout.md's fabricated blocks and
false empty-layout premise; nothing it named survives.

Also verified the position-aware receiver binding added in d6674403 from both
sides: a ghost injected after `const strip = new Strip(` fails naming Strip, the
same ghost after `const strip = new FlexStrip(` fails naming FlexStrip. Only the
second arm had been checked.

* test(docs): resolve every receiver shape, and let the checks fail on demand

Addresses all 10 findings from the second review round on PR #86. Four of them
were one defect seen from different angles: the gate silently checked less than
it appeared to.

RECEIVER SHAPES. `describeReceiver` handled a bare identifier and a call on a
property access, and dropped everything else — `if (!receiver) return;`, contrary
to its own docstring, which had claimed the caller reports rather than drops
since the function was written. Two live patterns fell through. `new
Table().addColumn("Name").addRow("Alice")` appears on docs/console.md twice and
neither member was ever checked; `progress.console.print` and
`live.console.print` were dropped because a getter receiver is a
PropertyAccessExpression. The chain base is genuinely two things — a variable
whose class needs looking up, or a constructor naming its class outright — so it
is a discriminated union now instead of a string the caller guessed about. A
property access became a hop like any other, which let the call case delegate to
it: the function covers three more shapes and is barely longer.

Resolution had to move with it. `returns` was built from `getCallSignatures()`,
empty for a getter, so fixing only the syntax would have produced a confident
"no class return type to follow". It is `yields` now: a method yields its return
type, anything else yields its own. One kind of hop.

TERMINUS. The chain loop checked every intermediate class for existence; the
terminus checked only ambiguity. A chain ending in a name this package does not
export returned as though resolved, and the ghost test's `if (!info || ...)`
turned that into a pass — two guards whose meanings cancelled. `resolveChain`
now returns the ClassInfo alongside the name, so holding a resolution *is* proof
the class exists and the downstream lookup is gone rather than duplicated. Both
existence and ambiguity moved into one `lookupType` used by the hops and the
terminus alike.

That check immediately failed on docs/widgets.md's `host.size().rows`, which is
correct — `TerminalSize` is an interface, and the surface map held classes only,
so the honest report read as a defect on a true page. Interfaces are in the map
now and `.rows` is genuinely checked.

AMBIGUITY was counting entry modules, not distinct classes. This repo re-exports
symbols from several entry points deliberately, so the first class re-exported
that way would have failed every page using it, and the obvious fix would have
looked like "stop re-exporting". `origins` is keyed by declaration identity.

`resolveSurface` also builds a program without `assertProgramClean`, which
`coverage.test.ts` calls for exactly this reason: a broken program answers short
instead of throwing, so a missing member reads as a real ghost.

THE DETECTORS NOW FAIL ON DEMAND. Every reachability assertion read `[]` off
correct data. Stubbing `danglingLinks` to `return []` leaves all seven of them
green — including "links no page that does not exist" — which is what a synthetic
fixture is for; the new one catches it. I had verified all three arms by
injection when I wrote them, but that ran against edited files and left no
artifact, so the repo could not tell the difference.

DOCS. progress.md's "a bar stuck at 0%" was mine from 5455a1f0 and was itself the
class-2 lie this suite's header warns about — a true statement about one path
generalized. Rendering a totalless task at completed 0/40/100/140 shows the two
columns disagree: the percentage freezes at 0% while BarColumn falls back to an
assumed total of 100, fills, and turns "finished". layout.md broke as a running
script: splitColumn assigns `this._children` wholesale, so "Fixed size" discarded
the upper/lower tree and "Ratio" then called splitRow on an undefined
getByName — the `!` silenced the compiler, not the runtime. The splitting
sections have their own root, and the whole block chain was executed in sequence
and type-checked rather than reasoned about. CLAUDE.md named the reachability
gate and not the symbol gate, omitting the more important of the two and its
resolution rule: red means the page is wrong, never that the library is missing
a feature.

Each new resolution path is verified by injection — a ghost on the fluent
constructor form names Table, on the getter hop names Console, on the interface
hop names TerminalSize — and the shapes are now asserted in the suite by the
class each must land on, since losing one leaves the total looking healthy.

* test(docs): resolve a receiver's class through the page's import aliases

Addresses 2 of 3 findings in review round 3 on PR #86. A chain's root class was
taken verbatim from the identifier after 'new', so 'import { Console as
RichConsole }' + 'new RichConsole()' gave rootClass RichConsole, a name
surfaceByName never heard of. Unrecognized receivers are dropped as someone
else's surface, so one alias would silently remove every member call on that
page from the check. ImportedName now carries 'local' beside 'name', and
extractMemberUses builds the alias map from importedNamesIn - the same walk that
answers the import check. Both root kinds resolve through it.

Also fixes a docstring naming exportsBySpecifier, gone since the programs merged;
it is exportedNames.

* test(docs): fixtures for the block parser, including shapes no page uses

The sweep in symbol-existence.test.ts asserts over the real pages, so it can
only pin receiver shapes some page happens to use today. A shape no page uses
costs it nothing: the bar stays green whether the parser handles that shape or
silently drops it.

That gap is measured, not argued. Reverting the import-alias resolution added in
the previous commit leaves all 19 existing docs tests green - including "follows
every receiver shape it recognizes" - and is caught only by the two alias arms
added here. It is the same shape as the earlier danglingLinks stub, which all
seven reachability tests survived.

code-blocks.ts reads no file and builds no compiler precisely so its rules can be
stated as markdown in, shape out. This is the file that spends that.

Covered: both fence spellings, the unterminated-fence throw, fence and use line
numbers, exported-vs-local import names, the namespace/default exclusion,
variable-to-constructor binding, a chain rooted in a constructor call, a getter
hop, a non-null assertion, nearest-preceding binding (Strip then FlexStrip), the
following-declaration fallback, both alias arms, and the string-literal and
comment cases the regex version once reported as defects.

Signatures are compared as a sorted set: the parser emits outermost-first, which
is a pre-order traversal artifact rather than anything a caller relies on.

* docs: a nesting section describing an outcome the library does not produce

"Nesting progress bars" showed two Progress instances both started, and closed
with "Inner bars refresh at the outer bar's refresh rate". Neither half is true.

Each Progress builds its own Live in its constructor with its own setInterval
(refreshPerSecond ?? 10) and, absent a console option, its own Console. Nothing
couples the timers, so there is no outer rate for the inner bar to adopt.

Worse, Live._clearLast emits ESC[1A ESC[2K exactly _lastLineCount times counting
up from wherever the cursor sits, knowing nothing of a second Live's output.
Captured from the byte stream of two started instances sharing a sink: the outer
writes Overall, the inner writes Batch below it, then the outer's next tick
clears upward from below Batch, erasing the inner bar and redrawing Overall in
its place. The display shows the outer bar twice and the inner never. The page
was not describing degraded nesting; the pictured outcome does not occur.

The motivation folds into the section two headings later, which already carried
the mechanism that works - one Live over a Group, none of the Progress instances
started, confirmed by rendering it. Retitled "Multiple progress displays at once"
and led with the constraint that explains both cases: one Progress gives every
task the same columns, and only one display may own the terminal at a time. The
corruption is documented at the close rather than deleted with the section.

The batch task is created once outside the loop and re-labelled through
updateTask, since a fresh addTask per batch leaves a finished row behind. It
counts percent, not items: a task's total is fixed at creation and
TaskUpdateOptions has no total field - the same constraint 5455a1f0 corrected
elsewhere on this page.

* test(docs): enumerate pages recursively, from one list both suites read

Both docs suites called readdirSync(DOCS_ROOT) without recursion, so a page in a
subdirectory of docs/ was absent from both sets - not excluded, invisible. The
scan that would have reported it was the scan that skipped it, so the bar stayed
green and nothing said the set was short.

docs/demos/index.md and docs/demos/[demo].md pass today by being unseen rather
than by being considered, and that distinction is the whole finding: a future
docs/advanced/foo.md linked from no sidebar region is exactly the silent orphan
docs/strip.md was for four commits, and a non-recursive scan cannot report it
because the page never enters the set being compared. Verified by adding such a
page: unreachablePages now names 'advanced/orphan', and did not before.

The enumeration moves into test/docs/pages.ts so the rule is stated once with
its reason, rather than a recursive scan and a demos/ filter copied into each
suite. demos/ is turned away by name with its argument attached - dynamic routes
from a gitignored manifest, no slug of their own - the same way sidebar.ts turns
away the Demos region instead of omitting it and hoping the omission reads as
deliberate.

* test(docs): scope alias resolution to our entry points, and order it

Resolving a receiver's class through the page's import aliases fixed a silent
drop and opened two ways to be confidently wrong instead.

An alias was translated no matter which module it came from. 'import { Layout as
X } from "some-other-lib"' followed by 'new X()' resolved X to *our* Layout, so a
third-party object's member calls were checked against a class they have nothing
to do with. Before the alias fix that receiver was dropped as someone else's
surface, which was the right answer; the fix turned a safe drop into a wrong
verdict. Only imports from the caller's entry-point set now bind.

The specifier set is a parameter rather than an import. code-blocks.ts is a
parser and does not know which specifiers are ours - the rule that knows holds
package.json - so putting ENTRY_BY_SPECIFIER in here would write that knowledge
in two places.

The alias map was also a flat last-one-wins Map, the same hazard already fixed
for variable declarations and left open for imports: a local name rebound to a
second class mid-page mis-checked the earlier section. Both are now Bindings -
one local name, one class name, one page position - resolved through a single
nearestBinding, so there is one page-ordering rule rather than two that can
disagree.

Fixtures cover both arms, since the corpus reaches neither: no page aliases an
import at all.

* test(docs): make chain resolution testable, then test the arms docs cannot reach

lookupType's ambiguity arm and resolveChain's dead-end and terminus-unresolved
arms had no test. They could not have one: both closed over the module-level
surfaceByName, so every branch was only ever reached with whatever the real
docs/ corpus contained - and it contains no ambiguous class name and no chain
that dead-ends. The conditions were evaluated, never taken.

Measured rather than argued. Inverting the ambiguity comparison to '< 1' leaves
all 37 existing docs tests green. Stubbing lookupType to always succeed leaves
symbol-existence's 8 green. Both are caught only by the new fixtures. That this
logic has already needed three separate fixes across one review is why the gap
mattered.

The failure it protects against is not a wrong message. The ghost check treats
an unresolved receiver as nothing to check, so a resolver that quietly stopped
rejecting reads exactly like a clean corpus.

Both functions move to test/docs/resolve-chain.ts taking the surface as a
parameter - the pure-module / sweep-module split page-reachability.ts and
code-blocks.ts already use here - so a synthetic surface can be handed to them.
The sweep passes the real one and reads the same.

* docs: build the sidebar from the composition the reachability gate reads

sidebar.ts exports pageSidebarRegions so there is one composed list of the
page-backed regions in order, and its header says so. config.ts imported nobody
and re-spread [...guideSidebar, ...advancedSidebar] beside the Demos entry - a
second composition of the same thing, one line below a header arguing against
exactly that.

The consequence is the failure the sidebar split was made to prevent, one level
up: a third page-backed region added to pageSidebarRegions but not to config's
spread (or the reverse) leaves the reachability gate checking a sidebar the site
does not render, and neither list can tell you which is lying.

Also corrects that header's attribution. It credited the assertion to
page-reachability.ts, which exports only detectors - linkedSlugs, danglingLinks,
unreachablePages, duplicateLinks - and contains no expect at all. The assertions
are in page-reachability.test.ts. The pure-module / sweep-module split is the
point of the pair, so misfiling the assertions undercuts the arrangement the
sentence is describing.

* docs: live.md claimed the nesting this PR just disproved for Progress

Progress is a thin wrapper over one Live, so deleting progress.md's nesting
section while live.md still said "Creating a Live inside an existing Live context
shows the inner content below the outer. Both can be updated independently" left
one mechanism described twice, in contradiction, with the false copy unmarked.

Verified by execution rather than inferred from the Progress case. Byte stream of
two Live instances started on one Console, escapes spelled out:

  [?25l [?25l OUTER-B\n INNER-B\n [1A [2K INNER-B\n [?25h [1A [2K OUTER-B\n [?25h

The inner Live clears and redraws its own line correctly. The outer then clears
one line up from where the cursor now sits - below the inner's line, not its own
- and writes its content there. The display ends showing the outer's content
twice and the inner's never. Both sentences were false.

The section is now "One Live owns the terminal": the constraint, the mechanism
(each Live clears its own last line count upward from the current cursor and
knows nothing of a second Live's output), and Group under a single Live as the
thing that does work. Its example imports the names it introduces, since the
page's own import block does not carry them.

progress.md's batch loop also went to for...of with await. Live refreshes on a
setInterval, so a synchronous forEach runs the whole batch in one turn of the
event loop and the bar snaps from 0 to 100 with nothing between - the example
would have demonstrated the opposite of its prose. An async handleItem was worse:
forEach drops the promise, so every item starts at once and completed runs ahead
of real work. await doStep(step) elsewhere on the page is the same shape.
